payload.title: Poetry Analysis: Spin Cycle, Ellery Street
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Spin Cycle, Ellery Street
by Marisol Teague

```passage
Eleven-forty. The change machine
eats my second five and gives back nothing,
and I let it, the way she let the landlord
keep the deposit every March.

Number nine is the only dryer that gets hot.
I learned that at seven, holding her coat
while she fed it quarters from a film can,
counting under her breath in two languages.

Her hands: chapped at the knuckle, a burn
shaped like a comma on the left thumb
from the press at Dunmore Cleaners,
a ring she turned inward so it wouldn't snag.

She folded a fitted sheet in the air
like a magician closing a box with a dove in it.
Nothing was ever lost. Nothing
was ever let go of, either.

Tomorrow the bus leaves at six.
I have packed the shirts she ironed
flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed
to a city she has never seen.

The drum turns. My clothes rise
and fall and rise, a slow tantrum
behind the round glass,
going nowhere at great speed.

I want to tell her: your hands
built me a door. I want to tell her:
I am walking out of it. Both are thank you.
Only one of them sounds like it.

The buzzer. Everything warm.
I fold the way she taught me, corners to corners,
and leave one sock in the lint trap,
so something of mine stays here, turning.
```

parts.prompt:
In the poem "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" (an original poem by Marisol Teague), the speaker waits out a wash cycle the night before leaving home and recalls the mother's hands at work.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Marisol Teague uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's complex attitude toward leaving, in which gratitude for the mother's labor is inseparable from a wish to escape the life that labor kept going.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
The night before she leaves home, the speaker of Marisol Teague's "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" sits in a laundromat doing exactly what her mother did for years, and the poem never gets past that irony. Teague uses the laundromat's circular imagery, the scarred details of the mother's hands, and line breaks that hold on and then let go to show that the speaker can only thank her mother by leaving her. Even the leaving is made out of the mother's habits. So gratitude and escape are not two separate feelings in this poem. They are one act seen from two sides.

The first stanza sets up this inheritance before the speaker admits it. When the change machine "eats my second five," she lets it, "the way she let the landlord / keep the deposit every March." The simile connects her to her mother's patience, but it is patience as giving up, and "every March" turns the loss into a yearly ritual. The memory of quarters fed from a film can, "counting under her breath in two languages," works the same way. The counting is careful and loving, the kind of labor that kept the family going, but it also shows how small and measured that life was, with every quarter tracked.

The third stanza is full of injury. The burn "shaped like a comma on the left thumb" stands out, because a comma is a pause and not a period. The mother's working life is a sentence that never gets to end. The ring "she turned inward so it wouldn't snag" suggests that even her one piece of jewelry, maybe her marriage, was turned to suit the job instead of her. Then the speaker admires her folding a sheet "like a magician closing a box with a dove in it." The image is full of wonder, but the dove is trapped. The line break that follows makes this tension happen on the page: "Nothing was ever lost. Nothing" ends the line, and the reader hangs on that second "Nothing" before the turn to "was ever let go of, either." What started as praise turns into complaint halfway through a sentence. Holding everything together and never letting anything go are the same act, and the enjambment forces us to feel both.

The shirts she ironed "flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed / to a city she has never seen" push this further. The mother's labor literally packages the speaker for departure, sending her child somewhere she herself could not go. The metaphor carries gratitude and guilt together. The dryer, meanwhile, is a "slow tantrum" with clothes "going nowhere at great speed." Calling it a tantrum gives the machine a child's frustration, which sounds like the speaker's own restlessness. The phrase also describes the mother's life, constant motion that stays in place. The repetition "rise / and fall and rise" copies the cycle the speaker is afraid of repeating.

The door metaphor is where the speaker comes closest to stating her attitude. Her repeated "I want to tell her" shows that she doesn't actually say it. Her mother's hands "built me a door," and "I am walking out of it." A reader could argue the mother is mainly confining, since she never let anything go, and the poem partly allows that reading. But a door is something the mother built, so the exit was in some sense her plan. That is why the speaker can say "Both are thank you" and also admit "Only one of them sounds like it." Leaving is the truer thanks, but it is the one her mother might not hear as thanks.

The ending refuses to settle this. The speaker folds "corners to corners," the way she was taught, so the mother's gestures go with her. Then she leaves a sock in the lint trap "so something of mine stays here, turning." This reverses "Nothing was ever lost": she deliberately lets something go, which her mother never did, but she does it so that part of her can stay. The last word, "turning," leaves her both gone and still in the cycle, which is where the poem has kept her all along.

rubric_rows.criterion: The thesis must make a defensible claim about the speaker's divided attitude, for example that gratitude for the mother's labor and the wish to escape are bound together. Saying the speaker 'misses her mother' or 'remembers the past' does not count, and neither does a list of devices. A thesis that names only one side can earn the point only if it is arguable and tied to how the poem presents leaving.

Strong responses use specific quotations such as the 'Nothing / was ever let go of' break, the 'door' metaphor, the 'slow tantrum' dryer, the envelope shirts, and the sock in the lint trap. The commentary must explain how each choice shows care that is also confinement, or departure that is also tribute. A score of 4 needs consistent links between evidence and the complex attitude across the poem. A score of 2 means the essay mostly summarizes or names devices with thin explanation.

Sophistication may show in tracing the speaker's inheritance of the mother's gestures (counting, folding) as a kind of continuity that complicates leaving. It may also show in reading the closing image as an unresolved ending, or in analyzing how line breaks enact holding on and letting go. Calling the poem 'complex' or using elevated vocabulary does not earn the point.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street," Marisol Teague shows a speaker who is leaving home and cannot separate being thankful to her mother from wanting to get away from the life her mother's work held up. The poem suggests that the same hard work that gave the speaker a future is also what she has to leave behind, so every thank you is also a goodbye.

The speaker's gratitude shows up first in the details about the mother's hands. They are "chapped at the knuckle" and have a burn "shaped like a comma" on the thumb. The comma is a nice image because a comma is a pause, not a stop, which could mean that the mother's work never really ends. These details make the mother's labor seem physical and real, and the speaker clearly respects it. The mother also "counting under her breath in two languages" shows how much effort she put into getting by. At the same time, the speaker remembers the landlord keeping the deposit "every March," which shows that the family was stuck in a cycle of being cheated and having little. The poem is about a laundromat, and the laundry is a good symbol of work that repeats.

The fourth stanza is where the mixed attitude is clearest. The speaker says the mother folded a sheet "like a magician closing a box with a dove in it." This is a loving comparison. Then the poem says "Nothing / was ever lost. Nothing / was ever let go of, either." The line break after "Nothing" makes the reader stop, and the word "either" turns the praise into a complaint. Holding on to everything is a kind of care, but it is also a kind of trap, and the speaker wants to be let go. The shirts "ironed flat as envelopes" are similar. They are a gift from the mother, but they are packed and "addressed to a city she has never seen," so the mother's work is literally being sent away from her.

The dryer image of the clothes as "a slow tantrum" that is "going nowhere at great speed" shows the speaker's frustration. The tone here is more bitter and a little funny, and it seems to describe the speaker's feelings about staying in the same place as well as the laundry. Then the metaphor "your hands / built me a door" is the main idea of the poem. The door was built by the mother, but the speaker is "walking out of it." The speaker says "Both are thank you. / Only one of them sounds like it," which admits that leaving might not look like gratitude even if it is.

The ending keeps both feelings. The speaker folds "the way she taught me" and leaves one sock in the lint trap "so something of mine stays here, turning." The folding shows the mother's influence continues, and the sock turning matches the drum, so the speaker is leaving but is not fully free of the cycle. The poem does not choose between the two feelings, which is why it feels honest.

In the first stanzas the speaker describes the laundromat. The change machine "eats my second five and gives back nothing" and this shows that the family did not have much money. The speaker also remembers holding her mother's coat at seven while she counted quarters. This is a memory of the mother working hard and the speaker watching her. The poet uses detail here to show the mother's life.

The third stanza is about the mother's hands. They are "chapped at the knuckle" and there is a burn from the cleaners. This imagery shows that the mother worked a lot and her hands were hurt by it. The speaker seems to respect her for this.

Later the speaker says she packed shirts that the mother ironed. They are "flat as envelopes" which is a simile. The speaker is going to a city her mother has never seen. Then the dryer is called a "slow tantrum" which shows the speaker is frustrated, like she is going nowhere.

At the end the speaker says "your hands built me a door" and that she is walking out of it. She leaves one sock in the lint trap. This shows she wants to leave but still wants something to stay. In conclusion the poet uses many techniques to show the speaker feels both thankful and wants to leave, which makes the poem about a complicated feeling.

It gives no arguable claim about how gratitude and the wish to escape are bound together, so it does not earn the thesis point.
- Row A: "which makes the poem about a complicated feeling" - The conclusion does name both thankfulness and wanting to leave, but it stops at calling the feeling 'complicated' with no interpretation to defend. The thesis point is still not earned.
- Row B: "this shows that the family did not have much money" - This is a general inference from the change machine. It does not link the image to the speaker's divided attitude, and it skips the echo of the landlord and deposit, so it is mostly summary.
- Row B: "This imagery shows that the mother worked a lot and her hands were hurt by it." - The quotation is relevant but the commentary only restates the detail. It does not explain how care is also confinement, for example in the ring turned inward.
- Row B: "which is a simile" - The device is named but its meaning is not explained. It misses that the sealed, addressed shirts turn the mother's labor into a message sent away, so the commentary stays thin.

It ignores the door metaphor's two meanings, 'Only one of them sounds like it,' and the 'turning' image, so there is no line of reasoning.

In "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street," Marisol Teague shows a speaker who is leaving home and cannot separate being thankful to her mother from wanting to get away from the life her mother's work held up. The poem suggests that the same hard work that gave the speaker a future is also what she has to leave behind, so every thank you is also a goodbye.

The speaker's gratitude shows up first in the details about the mother's hands. They are "chapped at the knuckle" and have a burn "shaped like a comma" on the thumb. The comma is a nice image because a comma is a pause, not a stop, which could mean that the mother's work never really ends. The mother also "counting under her breath in two languages" shows how much effort she put into getting by. At the same time, the speaker remembers the landlord keeping the deposit "every March," which shows that the family was stuck in a cycle of being cheated and having little. ALTON original passage
The Second Lesson
by Edmund Calloway Wrenne
This passage is from a novel published in 1861. Mr. Ashby, a newly engaged tutor of modest means, has come to the country house of the Pellingham family to instruct their eleven-year-old daughter, Clemency.

```passage
    Mrs. Pellingham received me in the morning-room,
which was warmed by two fires and furnished as if the
family expected at any hour to be inventoried. She
explained, with the patience of a woman describing a
weak chest, that her daughter was not quick. 'Clemency
is a dear, obliging creature,' she said, 'but she does
not take to figures, and French slides off her like rain
off a cabbage leaf. We ask only that she be made
presentable. Her sister was presentable at fourteen.'

    I bowed, and said that presentability was a worthy
object, and was conscious of having said something I
should be ashamed of before supper.

    The schoolroom lay at the end of a long passage hung
with portraits of Pellinghams in various attitudes of
having been painted. It was a cold room. Someone had
decided, at some remote date, that learning wanted no
fire, and the decision had hardened into a custom, as
decisions in that house did. The globe in the corner had
a dent in the Pacific where it had once been knocked
against the wainscot, and no one had thought the ocean
worth repairing.

    Clemency sat at the table with her hands folded upon
a slate. She was a thin child with a great deal of fair
hair arranged by someone else, and she looked at me with
the courteous blankness of a person waiting for a coach
that is late. I set her a sum in long division. She
considered it for a time, wrote a figure that was wrong,
and handed back the slate.

    'You see,' said her mother from the doorway, not
unkindly, and withdrew.

    I set her another. She wrote another wrong figure.
But I had been watching her pencil, and the pencil had
gone first to the correct answer and hovered there, as a
bird hovers over a field it means to cross, before it
turned aside and set down something a little stupider. I
said nothing. I gave her a third sum, harder than
either, and this time I turned my back and studied the
dented Pacific. When I looked again she had written the
answer, the true one, small in the corner, and was in
the very act of rubbing it out with the heel of her
hand.

    'That was right,' I said.

    She did not start. She only looked at the grey smear
on her palm, and then at me, and I understood that I had
been weighed, and that the scales were older than I was.
'Mamma says I have no head for it,' she said. 'Mamma is
generally right about heads. She has had a great deal of
practice.' There was no insolence in it. She said it the
way one reports the weather to a stranger who has walked
in from the rain and cannot be expected to know.

    I ought to have gone straight to Mrs. Pellingham. I
had been engaged, after all, to discover what the child
could do. Yet I thought of the morning-room and its two
fires, and of the sister who had been presentable at
fourteen and was now, I had been told at breakfast,
married to a gentleman in Shropshire who kept hounds. I
thought of what becomes of a clever girl in a house
where cleverness is a draught to be stopped with a
cushion. And I thought, I confess it, of my forty pounds
a year, and of how a tutor who reports a prodigy is soon
asked why his prodigy has not yet been made presentable.

    So we went on, she and I, through the long cold
winter, with two slates: one for the wrong answers,
which I showed her mother every Friday, and one for the
right ones, which Clemency kept beneath the cushion of
the window-seat. I flattered myself that I was her ally.
It was not until the spring, when the window-seat was
found empty and the slate gone with it, that I began to
suspect I had only been her accomplice, and that she had
been teaching me the whole while how to look away.
```

parts.prompt:
The following passage is an original work of fiction by Edmund Calloway Wrenne. In this passage, a young tutor discovers that his pupil hides her intelligence from her family and chooses to keep her secret.

Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Edmund Calloway Wrenne uses literary elements and techniques to convey the narrator's complex attitude toward the girl, her family, and his own role in her concealment.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
- Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
On a first reading, Mr. Ashby seems like the hero of his own story. He is the only adult in the Pellingham house who notices that Clemency is clever, and he is the one who protects her secret. But Wrenne does not let him keep that role. The passage uses Ashby's irony toward the family, the images he uses for Clemency, and the confessions he makes as an older narrator looking back. Together these show a man whose admiration for the girl and contempt for her family are real but tangled up with cowardice and self-interest. By the end, the missing slate shows that Ashby was never really the teacher, and his sympathy turns into a kind of self-indictment.

Ashby's attitude toward the Pellinghams comes mostly through dry irony. The morning-room is "furnished as if the family expected at any hour to be inventoried." That makes the family's comfort sound like a list of property, and the reader starts to suspect that Clemency is treated as one more item on it. Mrs. Pellingham describes her daughter "with the patience of a woman describing a weak chest." The simile turns slowness into an illness the family has bravely put up with. The schoolroom details push this further. Someone decided that "learning wanted no fire," while the morning-room has two fires, and the globe has a dent because no one "thought the ocean worth repairing." The dent is small, but it works as a symbol of the house: knowledge gets damaged and stays damaged because nobody values it. Still, Ashby is not mocking them from a safe distance. He tells Mrs. Pellingham that presentability is "a worthy object" and then immediately admits it was "something I should be ashamed of before supper." His irony is aimed at himself from the first page, which hints that he belongs to the system he criticizes.

Toward Clemency, Ashby's language becomes admiring, almost tender. Her pencil hovers over the right answer "as a bird hovers over a field it means to cross." The simile suggests freedom and intention. The bird "means" to cross, so the wrong answer is a choice, not a failure. But the admiration comes with unease. When he catches her, Ashby feels he has "been weighed," and that "the scales were older than I was." He is the adult, yet the child is doing the judging. Her remark that Mamma "has had a great deal of practice" at judging heads is so dry that it shows she understands her family better than he does. Ashby respects her, but he is also a little afraid of her.

The paragraph where Ashby decides to keep the secret is where his motives split open. He describes a house "where cleverness is a draught to be stopped with a cushion." The metaphor is sympathetic because it shows the family treating intelligence as an annoyance to be blocked out. Then he adds "I confess it" and mentions "my forty pounds a year." The word "confess" is the older narrator judging his younger self and admitting that pity and job security were working together. This is what makes the ending land so hard. The cushion comes back: Clemency keeps her real slate "beneath the cushion of the window-seat," which is the same object the family uses to stop up cleverness. By protecting her, Ashby helped her hide herself the way her family had always hidden her.

The final sentence turns everything around. Ashby "flattered" himself that he was her "ally" but comes to suspect he was only her "accomplice," and that she was "teaching me the whole while how to look away." A reader could see Clemency as manipulative here, using the tutor to cover her escape. I think it is more convincing to read her as self-protective, since she gets nothing from the trick except a hidden place to be right. Either way, the lesson in the title belongs to her. Ashby ends with admiration mixed with shame, because he realizes his kindness was also a way of looking away, which is exactly what the Pellinghams had been doing all along.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make a claim about the narrator's attitude that goes beyond a single feeling, for example admiration mixed with guilt or sympathy undercut by self-interest. Theses that only say the girl is smart and hides it, or that just restate the prompt, do not earn the point. The thesis can be anywhere in the response and may be more than one sentence.

Strong responses use specific evidence such as the hovering-bird simile, the dented globe, the draught-and-cushion metaphor, Clemency's 'great deal of practice' line, the two slates, and the 'accomplice' ending. Their commentary explains how each choice shapes the narrator's mixed attitude toward Clemency, the family, and himself. A score of 4 needs a consistent line of reasoning that tracks how his view changes. A score of 2 fits responses that mostly summarize or list techniques with thin explanation, and a score of 1 fits responses that only restate the text.

Sophistication can come from explaining the teacher-pupil reversal, the retrospective narrator judging his younger self, the cushion motif tying the family's suppression to Clemency's hiding place, or the tension between real sympathy and economic self-protection. Offhand phrases or a single complex sentence do not earn the point. The complexity has to run through the whole argument.

prompt.lead: The following passage is an original work of fiction by Edmund Calloway Wrenne. In this passage, a young tutor discovers that his pupil hides her intelligence from her family and chooses to keep her secret.
prompt.task: Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Edmund Calloway Wrenne uses literary elements and techniques to convey the narrator's complex attitude toward the girl, her family, and his own role in her concealment.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: The Second Lesson
passage.headnote: This passage is from a novel published in 1861. Mr. Ashby, a newly engaged tutor of modest means, has come to the country house of the Pellingham family to instruct their eleven-year-old daughter, Clemency.
stanzas: Mrs. Pellingham received me in the morning-room,
which was warmed by two fires and furnished as if the
family expected at any hour to be inventoried. She
explained, with the patience of a woman describing a
weak chest, that her daughter was not quick. 'Clemency
is a dear, obliging creature,' she said, 'but she does
not take to figures, and French slides off her like rain
off a cabbage leaf. We ask only that she be made
presentable. Her sister was presentable at fourteen.'
I bowed, and said that presentability was a worthy
object, and was conscious of having said something I
should be ashamed of before supper.
The schoolroom lay at the end of a long passage hung
with portraits of Pellinghams in various attitudes of
having been painted. It was a cold room. Someone had
decided, at some remote date, that learning wanted no
fire, and the decision had hardened into a custom, as
decisions in that house did. The globe in the corner had
a dent in the Pacific where it had once been knocked
against the wainscot, and no one had thought the ocean
worth repairing.
Clemency sat at the table with her hands folded upon
a slate. She was a thin child with a great deal of fair
hair arranged by someone else, and she looked at me with
the courteous blankness of a person waiting for a coach
that is late. I set her a sum in long division. She
considered it for a time, wrote a figure that was wrong,
and handed back the slate.
'You see,' said her mother from the doorway, not
unkindly, and withdrew.
I set her another. She wrote another wrong figure.
But I had been watching her pencil, and the pencil had
gone first to the correct answer and hovered there, as a
bird hovers over a field it means to cross, before it
turned aside and set down something a little stupider. I
said nothing. I gave her a third sum, harder than
either, and this time I turned my back and studied the
dented Pacific. When I looked again she had written the
answer, the true one, small in the corner, and was in
the very act of rubbing it out with the heel of her
hand.
'That was right,' I said.
She did not start. She only looked at the grey smear
on her palm, and then at me, and I understood that I had
been weighed, and that the scales were older than I was.
'Mamma says I have no head for it,' she said. 'Mamma is
generally right about heads. She has had a great deal of
practice.' There was no insolence in it. She said it the
way one reports the weather to a stranger who has walked
in from the rain and cannot be expected to know.
I ought to have gone straight to Mrs. Pellingham. I
had been engaged, after all, to discover what the child
could do. Yet I thought of the morning-room and its two
fires, and of the sister who had been presentable at
fourteen and was now, I had been told at breakfast,
married to a gentleman in Shropshire who kept hounds. I
thought of what becomes of a clever girl in a house
where cleverness is a draught to be stopped with a
cushion. And I thought, I confess it, of my forty pounds
a year, and of how a tutor who reports a prodigy is soon
asked why his prodigy has not yet been made presentable.
So we went on, she and I, through the long cold
winter, with two slates: one for the wrong answers,
which I showed her mother every Friday, and one for the
right ones, which Clemency kept beneath the cushion of
the window-seat. I flattered myself that I was her ally.
It was not until the spring, when the window-seat was
found empty and the slate gone with it, that I began to
suspect I had only been her accomplice, and that she had
been teaching me the whole while how to look away.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis must make a claim about the narrator's attitude that goes beyond a single feeling, for example admiration mixed with guilt or sympathy undercut by self-interest. Theses that only say the girl is smart and hides it, or that just restate the prompt, do not earn the point. The thesis can be anywhere in the response and may be more than one sentence.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses use specific evidence such as the hovering-bird simile, the dented globe, the draught-and-cushion metaphor, Clemency's 'great deal of practice' line, the two slates, and the 'accomplice' ending. Their commentary explains how each choice shapes the narrator's mixed attitude toward Clemency, the family, and himself. A score of 4 needs a consistent line of reasoning that tracks how his view changes. A score of 2 fits responses that mostly summarize or list techniques with thin explanation, and a score of 1 fits responses that only restate the text.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication can come from explaining the teacher-pupil reversal, the retrospective narrator judging his younger self, the cushion motif tying the family's suppression to Clemency's hiding place, or the tension between real sympathy and economic self-protection. Offhand phrases or a single complex sentence do not earn the point. The complexity has to run through the whole argument.

scoring_notes: Do not reward naming devices without explaining what they do.
Responses must deal with the narrator's attitude, not only Clemency's character.
Interpretations that read Clemency as manipulative or as self-protective are both acceptable if supported by the text.

defensible_positions: The narrator admires Clemency's concealed intelligence yet comes to see that his protection was compromised by self-interest, so his attitude mixes respect, guilt, and wry self-mockery.
Through satire of the Pellingham household the narrator presents Clemency's concealment as a rational survival strategy, while the ending exposes his own complicity in the same system.
The passage reverses the roles of teacher and pupil: the tutor who sets out to assess the child is himself assessed and instructed, which humbles his initial condescension.
The narrator's retrospective voice treats his younger self ironically, showing that his sympathy for Clemency was genuine but also flattering to himself.

devices.effect: Links the house's neglect of objects to its neglect of Clemency's mind.

Connect household images (two fires, cold schoolroom, cushion) to the family's values.
Analyze Clemency's speech and silence as evidence of her control.
Read the ending as a reversal recasting the whole relationship.
common_pitfalls: Summarizing the plot of the girl hiding her answers without analyzing the narrator's attitude.
Treating the narrator as simply heroic and ignoring the forty pounds and the word accomplice.
Calling Mrs. Pellingham merely cruel, missing the 'not unkindly' nuance and the satire of custom.
Listing devices without explaining how they shape the attitude.
Ignoring the ending's reversal.

samples.essay:
On a first reading, Mr. Ashby seems like the hero of his own story. He is the only adult in the Pellingham house who notices that Clemency is clever, and he is the one who protects her secret. But Wrenne does not let him keep that role. The passage uses Ashby's irony toward the family, the images he uses for Clemency, and the confessions he makes as an older narrator looking back. Together these show a man whose admiration for the girl and contempt for her family are real but tangled up with cowardice and self-interest. By the end, the missing slate shows that Ashby was never really the teacher, and his sympathy turns into a kind of self-indictment.

Ashby's attitude toward the Pellinghams comes mostly through dry irony. The morning-room is "furnished as if the family expected at any hour to be inventoried." That makes the family's comfort sound like a list of property, and the reader starts to suspect that Clemency is treated as one more item on it. Mrs. Pellingham describes her daughter "with the patience of a woman describing a weak chest." The simile turns slowness into an illness the family has bravely put up with. The schoolroom details push this further. Someone decided that "learning wanted no fire," while the morning-room has two fires, and the globe has a dent because no one "thought the ocean worth repairing." The dent is small, but it works as a symbol of the house: knowledge gets damaged and stays damaged because nobody values it. Still, Ashby is not mocking them from a safe distance. He tells Mrs. Pellingham that presentability is "a worthy object" and then immediately admits it was "something I should be ashamed of before supper." His irony is aimed at himself from the first page, which hints that he belongs to the system he criticizes.

Toward Clemency, Ashby's language becomes admiring, almost tender. Her pencil hovers over the right answer "as a bird hovers over a field it means to cross." The simile suggests freedom and intention. The bird "means" to cross, so the wrong answer is a choice, not a failure. But the admiration comes with unease. When he catches her, Ashby feels he has "been weighed," and that "the scales were older than I was." He is the adult, yet the child is doing the judging. Her remark that Mamma "has had a great deal of practice" at judging heads is so dry that it shows she understands her family better than he does. Ashby respects her, but he is also a little afraid of her.

The paragraph where Ashby decides to keep the secret is where his motives split open. He describes a house "where cleverness is a draught to be stopped with a cushion." The metaphor is sympathetic because it shows the family treating intelligence as an annoyance to be blocked out. Then he adds "I confess it" and mentions "my forty pounds a year." The word "confess" is the older narrator judging his younger self and admitting that pity and job security were working together. This is what makes the ending land so hard. The cushion comes back: Clemency keeps her real slate "beneath the cushion of the window-seat," which is the same object the family uses to stop up cleverness. By protecting her, Ashby helped her hide herself the way her family had always hidden her.

The final sentence turns everything around. Ashby "flattered" himself that he was her "ally" but comes to suspect he was only her "accomplice," and that she was "teaching me the whole while how to look away." A reader could see Clemency as manipulative here, using the tutor to cover her escape. I think it is more convincing to read her as self-protective, since she gets nothing from the trick except a hidden place to be right. Either way, the lesson in the title belongs to her. Ashby ends with admiration mixed with shame, because he realizes his kindness was also a way of looking away, which is exactly what the Pellinghams had been doing all along.

In "The Second Lesson," Edmund Calloway Wrenne presents a narrator whose attitude toward Clemency, her family, and himself is mixed. Mr. Ashby admires the girl and is critical of the Pellinghams, but he is also guilty about his own choices, because he keeps her secret partly out of sympathy and partly to protect his job. Through imagery, tone, and the structure of the passage, Wrenne shows a man who thinks he is being noble and slowly learns he was not.

At the start the narrator's attitude toward the family is mocking. The morning-room is "furnished as if the family expected at any hour to be inventoried," which makes the Pellinghams seem more concerned with possessions than with people. Mrs. Pellingham's comparison of French to "rain off a cabbage leaf" is ordinary and a little cold, and her repeated word "presentable" shows that she only cares about appearances. The narrator's own tone here is dry and ironic, and he admits that his agreement with her was something he "should be ashamed of before supper." This shows early that he is critical of others but also of himself, so he is not a simple hero.

The description of the schoolroom adds to this. The cold room and the dented globe suggest that the family does not care about learning, since "no one had thought the ocean worth repairing." The damaged Pacific works as a symbol of neglect, and the narrator seems to feel sorry for the child who has to learn there.

His admiration for Clemency appears in the simile of the pencil hovering "as a bird hovers over a field it means to cross." This image makes her seem graceful and intelligent, and it also suggests she is choosing to hold back instead of being unable. When she says her mother "has had a great deal of practice" at being right about heads, the narrator describes it as having "no insolence," which shows he respects her. He sees she is older than her years, because he feels "weighed" by her.

However, the narrator's reasons for staying quiet are not pure. He imagines a clever girl in a house where cleverness is "a draught to be stopped with a cushion," which is a metaphor that shows his sympathy. Then he adds "I confess it" before mentioning his "forty pounds a year." The confession shows that his sympathy is mixed with fear for his position, and the word "confess" tells us he is looking back and judging himself.

The ending makes this clearer. The two slates show the lie they keep up, and the cushion where Clemency hides the right answers repeats the cushion of the family's suppression. When the slate is gone, he realizes he was her "accomplice" and not her "ally," and that she had been teaching him "how to look away." The roles of teacher and pupil have turned around. In the end, the narrator admires Clemency, looks down on the family, and is ashamed of himself, because his silence helped the same system that he criticizes.

In many works of literature, a home is more than a setting. It can be a farmhouse that keeps a family alive through a hard winter, a crowded apartment where a grandmother's rules decide who may marry whom, or a ship's cabin, a convent cell, or a borrowed room that a refugee is told to be grateful for. The same walls that keep out danger can also keep a person in, and the comfort of belonging can carry obligations, silences, and limits. Writers often use such places to test what characters owe the people and structures that shelter them, and what it costs either to stay or to leave.

Either from your own reading or from the list below, choose a work of fiction in which a home, or a place that functions as one, both protects a character and confines that character. Then, in a well-written essay, analyze how the home and its double nature contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Do not merely summarize the plot.

- State a defensible thesis about how the idea in the prompt contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole.
- Support the argument with specific, accurate evidence from the work you chose, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Do not merely summarize the plot.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

In Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, the Helmer apartment seems like the safest place a woman in nineteenth-century Norway could hope to live. It is warm and decorated for Christmas, and Torvald's new job at the bank will pay for it. Ibsen builds the play so that every comfort the house gives Nora is also a rule she has to follow, though. The home protects her only while she agrees to be the person it was designed for, and the play suggests that a shelter built on one person's performance is really a stage. That is why Nora's exit at the end is both freedom and a real loss: the walls that kept her in were also the only self she had ever been allowed to have.

The first scene sets up this double meaning with small objects. Nora comes in with packages and a Christmas tree that she tells the maid to hide until it is decorated, and she secretly eats macaroons that Torvald has forbidden. The tree is a lot like Nora. It is something beautiful that gets arranged for display, and Torvald treats her the same way when he calls her by pet names for little birds and squirrels and hands her money as if it were an allowance. Even the macaroons matter. In this house even a cookie has to be hidden, so Nora has to lie to enjoy a harmless pleasure. Still, Ibsen does not pretend the protection is fake. When Mrs. Linde arrives, widowed, worn out, and desperate for work, she shows the audience what waits outside a husband's house for a woman with no money. Next to her, Nora's cage looks like luck, and I think that is the point. The comfort is real, which is exactly what makes it hard to leave.

The secret loan turns the house's logic upside down. Years earlier Nora borrowed money from Krogstad to pay for the trip to Italy that saved Torvald's life, so it turns out the home was being protected by her, not by him. But since a wife could not legally borrow without a man's consent, she forged her father's signature. The same social structure that is supposed to shelter women makes their own acts of protection criminal. Ibsen shows this through the locked letterbox. Krogstad drops his letter exposing the forgery into it, and only Torvald has the key, so a piece of the home meant for privacy becomes the trap closing on Nora. Her wild tarantella, danced to keep Torvald away from the mail, shows how little power she has. Performing is the one tool the house ever taught her to use.

The ending is where the two sides of the home separate. Torvald explodes at Nora, and then, once Krogstad sends back the bond, he forgives her and promises to shelter her like something he has rescued. His forgiveness is what shows Nora she has been a doll first in her father's house and then in her husband's, which makes the title refer to the whole institution rather than one marriage. Ibsen does not make her leaving easy, though. She walks out at night and leaves her children behind, and the nurse, Anne-Marie, who had to give away her own child to survive, reminds us that women in this world pay for every choice. Early audiences thought this was so shocking that Ibsen was pushed into writing a different ending for a German production in which Nora stays for the children. That reaction actually backs up the play's argument, because it shows how strongly people believed a home's protection should outweigh a woman's selfhood. The door slamming at the end is so powerful because it sounds like escape and like loss at once. Nora is free, but she has no shelter yet, and Ibsen leaves us unsure whether the world outside will be any kinder than the dollhouse.

In Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, the Helmer home is a place that looks like safety but works like a cage. By the end, her leaving shows that a home built on someone's dependence cannot actually belong to her.

At the start of the play the home seems warm and protective. It is Christmas, Nora comes in with packages, and Torvald talks to her from his study like a pleased parent. He calls her pet names such as "little lark" and "squirrel," and these seem affectionate. The household has money coming in because Torvald is about to become a bank manager, so it appears to shelter Nora from the worries of the outside world. However, the nicknames also treat her like an animal or a child and not like an equal. The comfort of the home depends on Nora staying small and sweet, and this is the first sign that protection and confinement are the same thing. The stage setting of one living room, where almost the whole play takes place, also makes the home feel closed in.

The confinement becomes clearer once Nora's secret is brought in. Years before, she borrowed money by forging her father's signature to save Torvald's life, and she has hidden it in order to keep the peace of the house. She has to sneak macaroons and hide things from him, which shows that the home has rules she cannot openly break. The tarantella scene is another good example. Torvald makes her practice the dance and controls how she performs it, so even her body is directed by him. The house is a stage where Nora performs the role of the happy wife, and the title's image of a doll fits because a doll is kept safe only as long as it does what its owner wants.

The turning point is when Torvald reads Krogstad's letter and reacts by caring only about his reputation, not about what Nora did for him. He calls her names and says she is not fit to raise the children, but when the danger passes he wants to go back to normal. This shows that the protection he offered was always conditional. When Nora decides to leave, the slamming door at the end ends the play and is a symbol for her choice. Her departure is not simply freedom, because she leaves her children and the only security she has known, so it costs her a great deal.

prompt.lead: In many works of literature, a home is more than a setting. It can be a farmhouse that keeps a family alive through a hard winter, a crowded apartment where a grandmother's rules decide who may marry whom, or a ship's cabin, a convent cell, or a borrowed room that a refugee is told to be grateful for. The same walls that keep out danger can also keep a person in, and the comfort of belonging can carry obligations, silences, and limits. Writers often use such places to test what characters owe the people and structures that shelter them, and what it costs either to stay or to leave.

lines_of_reasoning: Protection and confinement are one force: the thing that keeps a character safe (isolation, strict rules, a remote location) is exactly what limits growth. Fits a novel about a sheltered daughter on an isolated estate, or a gothic novel set in a crumbling family mansion.

Home as inheritance and duty: a character stays to keep up a family house or business, and loyalty becomes a trap. Fits family sagas, plays about a declining family farm, or immigrant novels about a family shop.

Gendered domestic space: the house protects a woman's status while limiting her to roles defined by others. Fits nineteenth-century domestic novels, a play about a wife in a well-run household, or postcolonial stories of courtyard homes.

Home as refuge from a hostile outside world: for a persecuted or displaced character, the hiding place or community saves a life but cuts the character off from a full self. Fits wartime hiding narratives, novels about enslaved people escaping, or stories of exile communities.

Leaving as both liberation and loss: the departure frees the character but cuts the roots that formed them, so the ending is ambivalent. Fits coming-of-age novels about leaving a village for a city, or migration stories.
The character becomes the confining force: someone once sheltered goes on to enforce the same walls on the next generation. Fits multigenerational novels and plays about parents and children.

Home as a mental structure: a belief system, a memory, or an idealized past acts as a home that comforts and imprisons. Fits novels about characters stuck in nostalgia, or dystopian fiction where a protected city limits thought.
Institutions as homes: a school, a ship, a monastery, or an asylum gives order and safety while erasing individuality. Fits boarding-school novels, sea narratives, or novels set in hospitals.
defensible_positions: The home's protection is real, but the work suggests its price, which is a character's selfhood, is too high, and escape becomes necessary.
The work refuses a simple verdict: the character's confinement and safety cannot be separated, which shows that belonging always involves constraint.
The confinement is only visible from the inside after a crisis, which suggests that comfort hides the walls until something threatens them.
Leaving the home doesn't solve anything, because the character carries its limits along; the true enclosure is internal.
common_pitfalls: Retelling the plot of the work without connecting events to the home's protective and confining sides.
Talking about only one side (the home as purely a prison or purely a refuge) and ignoring the double nature the prompt asks for.
Forcing a work to fit by calling any setting a 'home' without showing that it works as a place of belonging or shelter.
Writing about the concept in general or using several works, instead of developing one work in depth.
Saying the home is 'complex' without explaining how that complexity shapes a meaning of the whole work.
Ending with a moral about real homes instead of a claim about the chosen work.

In Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, the Helmer home is a place that looks like safety but works like a cage. Ibsen uses the house to show that the comfort Nora gets from her marriage is bought with her freedom, so that the protection she receives is really a form of control. By the end, her leaving shows that a home built on someone's dependence cannot actually belong to her.

At the start of the play the home seems warm and protective. It is Christmas, Nora comes in with packages, and Torvald talks to her from his study like a pleased parent. He calls her pet names such as "little lark" and "squirrel," and these seem affectionate. The household has money coming in because Torvald is about to become a bank manager, so it appears to shelter Nora from the worries of the outside world. However, the nicknames also treat her like an animal or a child and not like an equal. The comfort of the home depends on Nora staying small and sweet, and this is the first sign that protection and confinement are the same thing. The stage setting of one living room, where almost the whole play takes place, also makes the home feel closed in.

The confinement becomes clearer once Nora's secret is brought in. Years before, she borrowed money by forging her father's signature to save Torvald's life, and she has hidden it in order to keep the peace of the house. She has to sneak macaroons and hide things from him, which shows that the home has rules she cannot openly break. The tarantella scene is another good example. Torvald makes her practice the dance and controls how she performs it, so even her body is directed by him. payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End
by Tobias Wrenfield
The Ellery farm in the poem is a fictional property. Old Ellery is its owner; the speaker is a hired hand.

```passage
You know my hands better than his ledger does.
Nine Marches I have climbed into your crotches
with the pruning hook and the tin of grafting wax,
and cut you back to the bone so you would bear.

Old Ellery walks you Sundays in his collar.
He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar.
There is the Baldwin I split and bound with twine
the winter the creek froze down to its stones;
it leans now like a man who has been told a joke
he did not like, and keeps it to himself.

Bear, then. Bear for him. You never asked
whose ladder leaned against you in the frost,
whose knee was bruised blue on your lowest limb.
A tree is a poor Christian. It forgives
nobody, and it thanks nobody, and it goes on.

Still, I made you. Say it, if a tree can say.
Not the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank,
not the man in the buggy with the gold-toothed wife:
I made you as a man makes a stubborn son,
by hitting where it hurt and staying near.

Tomorrow they will pay me off in silver
and the cider press will groan like a cow in calf,
and I will walk the road toward Hatch's Mill
with my coat over my arm and nothing in it.

But when your apples sit in some city bowl,
red as a slapped cheek on a parlor table,
and a lady turns one in her gloves and says how fine,
let one of them, just one, be sour at the core.
Let her taste me.
```

parts.prompt:
In the poem "To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End" (an original poem by Tobias Wrenfield), the speaker talks to the apple orchard he has pruned, grafted and picked for another man's profit, on the last evening of the harvest.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Tobias Wrenfield uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's complex attitude toward the orchard, in which pride of craft and a claim of kinship sit alongside grievance at being dispossessed of what his labor made.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
The speaker of "To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End" has done everything a father does for a child except own it. Tobias Wrenfield's hired hand speaks to the trees on his last night as if they were family, but every claim of kinship he makes runs into the fact that the law, the bank, and Old Ellery have the stronger claim. Wrenfield uses a contrast between bodily and commercial language, a shift in how the speaker addresses the orchard, and a final curse that is also a plea to be remembered. Together they show that the speaker's pride in his work is exactly what makes losing it hurt. He cannot be proud of the orchard without also being bitter about it.

From the first line the poem sets two ways of knowing the orchard against each other. "You know my hands better than his ledger does" puts the speaker's body next to Ellery's book, and the speaker obviously thinks the hands win. The same split comes back in the sharpest line of the second stanza: "He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar." The parallel grammar makes the two men equal for a second, since each one is counting, but what they count is completely different. A bushel is a unit you sell. A scar is something the tree and the man both carry, so the word quietly makes them alike. The Baldwin he "split and bound with twine" was healed the way a broken arm is set. The simile that it "leans now like a man who has been told a joke" gives the tree a person's private resentment, but that resentment is really the speaker's, and he can only express it by lending it to the tree.

The third stanza turns the address sour: "Bear, then. Bear for him." The imperative sounds like permission but reads like an accusation, and the repeated "bear" carries two meanings, bearing fruit and bearing a burden. He complains that the tree "never asked" whose knee was bruised, then admits "A tree is a poor Christian." The line is half a joke, but it shows the speaker knows his grievance has nowhere to go. A tree cannot thank him, and he implies that the man who owns it won't either.

Then comes the turn: "Still, I made you." The word "Still" takes back everything the previous stanza conceded. The repeated negatives, "Not the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank," list the legal and financial powers that own the orchard only so he can dismiss them. This is where the poem's paradox is clearest. Through his labor the orchard is his, but legally it is not, and he can only assert the first claim by naming the second. The simile "I made you as a man makes a stubborn son" is followed by "by hitting where it hurt and staying near," which may be the most honest moment in the poem. It admits the kinship was built through violence, the same pruning that cut the trees "back to the bone." His love was never gentle, and that makes it more believable.

The fifth stanza's plain, almost flat language shows what being dispossessed looks like. He walks toward Hatch's Mill "with my coat over my arm and nothing in it," paid in silver but still empty-handed. That emptiness sets up the ending. The apple "red as a slapped cheek on a parlor table" carries the violence of the son simile into the lady's parlor, as if the fruit still holds the mark of the hand that raised it. When he asks that one apple "be sour at the core," it is easy to read the line as pure revenge. But the last line, "Let her taste me," changes it. He is not only spoiling her pleasure. He wants to be inside the fruit, noticed by someone who will never know his name. The curse is the only signature a hired man can leave.

Wrenfield's speaker never resolves his feelings, and that is the point. The pride and the grievance come out of the same nine Marches of work, so the closer he gets to claiming the orchard, the more clearly he sees that he has lost it.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the speaker's attitude holds both pride or kinship and grievance or dispossession, e.g., that his authorship sharpens his loss. Merely saying the speaker loves the orchard, or that the poem uses imagery and simile, does not count. A thesis naming only one side of the attitude earns the point only if it is defensible and interprets the poem rather than restating it.

Strong responses cite specific lines such as 'He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar,' the turn 'Still, I made you,' the stubborn-son simile, and the sour core, and explain how each builds the tension between pride and grievance. Commentary should connect bodily diction against commercial diction, or the poem's movement in address, to the speaker's complex attitude. A score of 4 requires consistent explanation of how choices create meaning across the poem; 2 marks mostly summary with general comments on devices; 3 links evidence to the claim but unevenly.

Sophistication may come from exploring the paradox that labor makes the orchard his in spirit and not his in law, from reading the final lines as both curse and wish to be remembered, or from setting the poem in the context of hired labor and land ownership without leaving the text. A single phrase or broad statement does not earn the point; the complexity must be sustained.

In "To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End," Tobias Wrenfield presents a speaker who is proud of what his hands have done and who feels the orchard is almost family, but who is also bitter that none of it belongs to him. The poem shows that the more the speaker claims the orchard through his work, the more painful it is that he has to leave it.

The speaker's pride shows up first in the way he describes his work in physical terms. He says "You know my hands better than his ledger does," which sets the orchard's knowledge of him against the owner's paperwork. Right away the poem sets up a contrast between the body and money. The speaker has climbed "into your crotches" and cut the trees "back to the bone," and these words make the work sound hard and personal. The line "He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar" is the clearest example. The parallel structure makes the two men equals on the page, but the words are different. Bushel is a commercial word and scar is a bodily one, so the speaker seems to be saying that his way of counting is the more real one. The image of the Baldwin tree that "leans now like a man who has been told a joke" he did not like is also a sign of pride, because the speaker gives the tree a human personality, as if he knows it like a person.

The poem then turns at "Still, I made you." Before this the speaker tells the orchard to "Bear for him," which sounds tired and resigned, and he says a tree "forgives nobody." The word "Still" shows he cannot stay resigned. The simile that he made the orchard "as a man makes a stubborn son, / by hitting where it hurt and staying near" is where the kinship claim is strongest. It is also a little harsh, since it admits that the care involved pain. This makes the claim feel honest rather than sentimental. At the same time the speaker lists what he does not have, "the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank," so the legal side of ownership is shown to be against him.

The last line can be read as revenge, but it can also be read as a wish to be remembered, since he wants part of himself to stay in the orchard's fruit.

lit_frq.title: To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End

prompt.lead: In the poem "To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End" (an original poem by Tobias Wrenfield), the speaker talks to the apple orchard he has pruned, grafted and picked for another man's profit, on the last evening of the harvest.
prompt.task: Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Tobias Wrenfield uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's complex attitude toward the orchard, in which pride of craft and a claim of kinship sit alongside grievance at being dispossessed of what his labor made.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End
passage.headnote: The Ellery farm in the poem is a fictional property. Old Ellery is its owner; the speaker is a hired hand.
stanzas: You know my hands better than his ledger does.
Nine Marches I have climbed into your crotches
with the pruning hook and the tin of grafting wax,
and cut you back to the bone so you would bear.
Old Ellery walks you Sundays in his collar.
He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar.
There is the Baldwin I split and bound with twine
the winter the creek froze down to its stones;
it leans now like a man who has been told a joke
he did not like, and keeps it to himself.
Bear, then. Bear for him. You never asked
whose ladder leaned against you in the frost,
whose knee was bruised blue on your lowest limb.
A tree is a poor Christian. It forgives
nobody, and it thanks nobody, and it goes on.
Still, I made you. Say it, if a tree can say.
Not the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank,
not the man in the buggy with the gold-toothed wife:
I made you as a man makes a stubborn son,
by hitting where it hurt and staying near.
Tomorrow they will pay me off in silver
and the cider press will groan like a cow in calf,
and I will walk the road toward Hatch's Mill
with my coat over my arm and nothing in it.
But when your apples sit in some city bowl,
red as a slapped cheek on a parlor table,
and a lady turns one in her gloves and says how fine,
let one of them, just one, be sour at the core.
Let her taste me.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the speaker's attitude holds both pride or kinship and grievance or dispossession, e.g., that his authorship sharpens his loss. Merely saying the speaker loves the orchard, or that the poem uses imagery and simile, does not count. A thesis naming only one side of the attitude earns the point only if it is defensible and interprets the poem rather than restating it.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses cite specific lines such as 'He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar,' the turn 'Still, I made you,' the stubborn-son simile, and the sour core, and explain how each builds the tension between pride and grievance. Commentary should connect bodily diction against commercial diction, or the poem's movement in address, to the speaker's complex attitude. A score of 4 requires consistent explanation of how choices create meaning across the poem; 2 marks mostly summary with general comments on devices; 3 links evidence to the claim but unevenly.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication may come from exploring the paradox that labor makes the orchard his in spirit and not his in law, from reading the final lines as both curse and wish to be remembered, or from setting the poem in the context of hired labor and land ownership without leaving the text. A single phrase or broad statement does not earn the point; the complexity must be sustained.

scoring_notes: Accept readings that emphasize love over bitterness, or the reverse, if they account for the other side.
Do not reward naming devices without analysis.
Historical context is optional and must serve the analysis.

defensible_positions: The speaker's pride in his craft deepens rather than softens his grievance, since the better he made the orchard the more he loses by leaving it.
The poem sets bodily, felt knowledge against legal and commercial ownership, claiming the laborer as the orchard's true author while admitting he has no power.
The speaker's love for the orchard is fatherly and violent at once, so his parting words are both a blessing and a curse.
The speaker's resentment moves from owner to orchard to the distant consumer, showing that dispossession taints even what he loves.

devices.effect: Opposes profit and pain as two ways of knowing the trees.

devices.quote: Still, I made you.
devices.effect: Moves from bitterness to an assertion of pride and authorship.

devices.quote: as a man makes a stubborn son
devices.effect: Kinship that holds both love and harshness.

devices.quote: A tree is a poor Christian.
devices.effect: Shows the orchard is indifferent; he cannot even claim its gratitude.

devices.quote: nothing in it
devices.effect: Being paid off leaves him with nothing.

devices.quote: sour at the core
devices.effect: His lasting stake is a hidden grievance inside the fruit.

common_pitfalls: Reading the poem as simple nature appreciation or simple protest, missing the divided attitude.
Listing devices without explaining how they create the tension between pride and grievance.
Treating the final lines as pure spite, ignoring that the sour apple is also a wish to be remembered.
Summarizing the stanzas in order without a claim.
lines_of_reasoning: Trace the shift in address from intimacy, to the owner, to the orchard's indifference, to authorship, to the curse.
Analyze the bodily diction (hands, scar, knee, bone) set against money diction (ledger, bushel, deed, bank, silver).

samples.essay:
The speaker of "To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End" has done everything a father does for a child except own it. Tobias Wrenfield's hired hand speaks to the trees on his last night as if they were family, but every claim of kinship he makes runs into the fact that the law, the bank, and Old Ellery have the stronger claim. Wrenfield uses a contrast between bodily and commercial language, a shift in how the speaker addresses the orchard, and a final curse that is also a plea to be remembered. Together they show that the speaker's pride in his work is exactly what makes losing it hurt. He cannot be proud of the orchard without also being bitter about it.

From the first line the poem sets two ways of knowing the orchard against each other. "You know my hands better than his ledger does" puts the speaker's body next to Ellery's book, and the speaker obviously thinks the hands win. The same split comes back in the sharpest line of the second stanza: "He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar." The parallel grammar makes the two men equal for a second, since each one is counting, but what they count is completely different. A bushel is a unit you sell. A scar is something the tree and the man both carry, so the word quietly makes them alike. The Baldwin he "split and bound with twine" was healed the way a broken arm is set. The simile that it "leans now like a man who has been told a joke" gives the tree a person's private resentment, but that resentment is really the speaker's, and he can only express it by lending it to the tree.

The third stanza turns the address sour: "Bear, then. Bear for him." The imperative sounds like permission but reads like an accusation, and the repeated "bear" carries two meanings, bearing fruit and bearing a burden. He complains that the tree "never asked" whose knee was bruised, then admits "A tree is a poor Christian." The line is half a joke, but it shows the speaker knows his grievance has nowhere to go. A tree cannot thank him, and he implies that the man who owns it won't either.

Then comes the turn: "Still, I made you." The word "Still" takes back everything the previous stanza conceded. The repeated negatives, "Not the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank," list the legal and financial powers that own the orchard only so he can dismiss them. This is where the poem's paradox is clearest. Through his labor the orchard is his, but legally it is not, and he can only assert the first claim by naming the second. The simile "I made you as a man makes a stubborn son" is followed by "by hitting where it hurt and staying near," which may be the most honest moment in the poem. It admits the kinship was built through violence, the same pruning that cut the trees "back to the bone." His love was never gentle, and that makes it more believable.

The fifth stanza's plain, almost flat language shows what being dispossessed looks like. He walks toward Hatch's Mill "with my coat over my arm and nothing in it," paid in silver but still empty-handed. That emptiness sets up the ending. The apple "red as a slapped cheek on a parlor table" carries the violence of the son simile into the lady's parlor, as if the fruit still holds the mark of the hand that raised it. When he asks that one apple "be sour at the core," it is easy to read the line as pure revenge. But the last line, "Let her taste me," changes it. He is not only spoiling her pleasure. He wants to be inside the fruit, noticed by someone who will never know his name. The curse is the only signature a hired man can leave.

Wrenfield's speaker never resolves his feelings, and that is the point. The pride and the grievance come out of the same nine Marches of work, so the closer he gets to claiming the orchard, the more clearly he sees that he has lost it.

In "To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End," Tobias Wrenfield presents a speaker who is proud of what his hands have done and who feels the orchard is almost family, but who is also bitter that none of it belongs to him. The poem shows that the more the speaker claims the orchard through his work, the more painful it is that he has to leave it.

The speaker's pride shows up first in the way he describes his work in physical terms. He says "You know my hands better than his ledger does," which sets the orchard's knowledge of him against the owner's paperwork. Right away the poem sets up a contrast between the body and money. The speaker has climbed "into your crotches" and cut the trees "back to the bone," and these words make the work sound hard and personal. The line "He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar" is the clearest example. The parallel structure makes the two men equals on the page, but the words are different. Bushel is a commercial word and scar is a bodily one, so the speaker seems to be saying that his way of counting is the more real one. The image of the Baldwin tree that "leans now like a man who has been told a joke" he did not like is also a sign of pride, because the speaker gives the tree a human personality, as if he knows it like a person.

The poem then turns at "Still, I made you." Before this the speaker tells the orchard to "Bear for him," which sounds tired and resigned, and he says a tree "forgives nobody." The word "Still" shows he cannot stay resigned. The simile that he made the orchard "as a man makes a stubborn son, / by hitting where it hurt and staying near" is where the kinship claim is strongest. It is also a little harsh, since it admits that the care involved pain. This makes the claim feel honest rather than sentimental. At the same time the speaker lists what he does not have, "the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank," so the legal side of ownership is shown to be against him.

The ending shows the grievance most openly. He will walk to Hatch's Mill "with my coat over my arm and nothing in it," which is a plain image of being left with nothing. Then he asks that one apple be "sour at the core" so the lady will "Let her taste me." The apple is a simile for a slapped cheek, so even the beauty of the fruit is tied to violence. The last line can be read as revenge, but it can also be read as a wish to be remembered, since he wants part of himself to stay in the orchard's fruit.

Overall, Wrenfield uses diction, simile, and a shift in tone to show that the speaker's craft gives him a real claim to the orchard that the law does not recognize, and this is why his loss hurts so much.
