payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
The Letter on the Net Box
by Orla Bressan
In this excerpt from the novel Salt Hours, Nell Garrow, nineteen, works with her widowed father, Amos, on the shingle below their village. She has applied for a clerk's position in the city.

```passage
    The letter had come on Tuesday and it was Thursday
now, and still it lay on the lid of the net box with a
beach stone on it, a gray stone with a white band around
its middle like a wedding ring somebody had forgotten to
take off. Nell had put the stone there herself. The wind
off the point would have had the envelope otherwise, and
she told herself that was the only reason.

    Her father sat on an upturned crate with the trammel
net across his knees, and she sat on the shingle with
the other end of it across hers, so that the two of them
were joined by forty feet of brown mesh and the holes
the dogfish had made. He did not look at the letter. He
looked at the net. He had a way of looking at a net that
made it seem the whole sea had been arranged to pass
through it eventually.

    "Mind your knots," he said.

    "I am minding them."

    "You're pulling them. A pulled knot slips in cold
water." He reached over without getting up and took the
twine from her fingers and made the knot again, sheet
bend, a quick small violence of the thumbs, and gave the
twine back. His hands were split along every crease, and
in the splits was the tar from the boat, so that his
palms looked like maps of a country with too many
rivers.

    She mended. The needle went over, under, through.
Over, under, through. Out past the breakwater the Callie
and the Ruth Ann were coming in low, and gulls hung
above them as if on strings. Her mother had used to say
you could tell a boat's catch from the shore by how the
gulls behaved. Her mother had used to say a good many
things. Nell had been eleven when the saying stopped,
and since then the house had run on her father's few
words and the clock and the kettle, and she had learned
to fill the rest of the quiet herself, the way you learn
to fill a hole in a net, by working inward from the
sound edges.

    The envelope was cream, heavier than anything that
came to the village, with the name of the shipping
office printed blue in the corner: Harlan and Vey, Cargo
Agents, Dock Street. She knew what it said. Or she knew
it said one of two things, and either one would be a
door, and she did not know which side of the door she
wanted to be standing on. If it said no, she could keep
the stone on it forever. If it said yes, someone would
have to tell him, and the someone would be her.

    "Ruth Ann's heavy," her father said.

    "Is she?"

    "Look at her waterline." He jerked his chin. "Dan
Pruett will want hands Saturday for the gutting. I told
him you'd come."

    He had told Dan Pruett. Of course he had. He had
told Dan Pruett on Tuesday, probably, the same afternoon
the postman came down the cliff path, waving the cream
envelope above his head like a flag for her to see from
the beach, and her father had watched him come all the
way down and said nothing at all. Saturday. He had built
her a Saturday and set it on the calendar like a stone
on a letter.

    She could have been angry. She tried it for a
moment, the way you try a plank before you put your
weight on it, and found it would not hold. Because he
was not wrong about her knots. Because the net in her
lap was one she had mended every spring since she was
nine, and she knew it the way she knew her own teeth
with her tongue. Because when he took the twine from her
fingers his own fingers had been warm, and she had
wanted, absurdly, for him to keep holding it.

    The tide turned at four. The wind came round and
lifted one corner of the envelope, and it fluttered
under the stone like something breathing. Her father's
needle stopped. Nell watched his hands lie still on the
mesh for the space of three waves. Then they began
again, over, under, through, and he said, not looking
up, "You'll want to read that before the light goes."

    "Tomorrow," she said.

    He nodded as though she had told him the weather.
She pulled the next knot tight, too tight, and did not
let him see her loosen it.
```

parts.prompt:
The following passage is an original work of fiction by Orla Bressan. In this passage, a young woman mends fishing nets beside her father while a letter from the city waits, unopened, on the box between them.

Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Orla Bressan uses literary elements and techniques to convey the daughter's divided feelings about the letter and about the father whose work and silence hold her in place.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
- Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
In this passage from Salt Hours, Nell Garrow goes two days without opening a letter that could take her to the city, and Bressan makes it clear that Nell is keeping it shut as much as her father is. Through images of weighting and binding, the repeated rhythm of mending, and a small gesture Nell hides at the end, Bressan shows that Nell resents her father's silent way of deciding her life but loves him too much, and is too shaped by his work, to fight him openly. Because of this, staying and leaving both feel like kinds of being tied down, and the only rebellion she can manage is a private one.

The passage opens with the letter weighted by a stone with a white band, "like a wedding ring somebody had forgotten to take off." It's a strange simile for a girl thinking about a clerk's job, but it fits. A forgotten ring is a promise that has outlasted its reason, and it could stand for her parents' marriage after her mother's death or for Nell's own unspoken promise to this beach. Then the narrator says Nell put the stone there herself, and "she told herself that was the only reason." The words "told herself" show she doesn't quite believe her own excuse. The irony is that the thing pinning down her future is something she put there. Later, when she learns her father promised her to Dan Pruett, she thinks "He had built her a Saturday" and set it down "like a stone on a letter." Bressan repeats the image so that Nell's accusation hits her too. She is angry at him for doing exactly what she did, which is why her resentment can never stay pure.

The net is the main image of how the two are tied together. They are "joined by forty feet of brown mesh," which is connection and entanglement at once. passage.title: The Letter on the Net Box
passage.headnote: In this excerpt from the novel Salt Hours, Nell Garrow, nineteen, works with her widowed father, Amos, on the shingle below their village. She has applied for a clerk's position in the city.
stanzas: The letter had come on Tuesday and it was Thursday
now, and still it lay on the lid of the net box with a
beach stone on it, a gray stone with a white band around
its middle like a wedding ring somebody had forgotten to
take off. Nell had put the stone there herself. The wind
off the point would have had the envelope otherwise, and
she told herself that was the only reason.
Her father sat on an upturned crate with the trammel
net across his knees, and she sat on the shingle with
the other end of it across hers, so that the two of them
were joined by forty feet of brown mesh and the holes
the dogfish had made. He did not look at the letter. He
looked at the net. He had a way of looking at a net that
made it seem the whole sea had been arranged to pass
through it eventually.
"Mind your knots," he said.
"I am minding them."
"You're pulling them. A pulled knot slips in cold
water." He reached over without getting up and took the
twine from her fingers and made the knot again, sheet
bend, a quick small violence of the thumbs, and gave the
twine back. His hands were split along every crease, and
in the splits was the tar from the boat, so that his
palms looked like maps of a country with too many
rivers.
She mended. The needle went over, under, through.
Over, under, through. Out past the breakwater the Callie
and the Ruth Ann were coming in low, and gulls hung
above them as if on strings. Her mother had used to say
you could tell a boat's catch from the shore by how the
gulls behaved. Her mother had used to say a good many
things. Nell had been eleven when the saying stopped,
and since then the house had run on her father's few
words and the clock and the kettle, and she had learned
to fill the rest of the quiet herself, the way you learn
to fill a hole in a net, by working inward from the
sound edges.
The envelope was cream, heavier than anything that
came to the village, with the name of the shipping
office printed blue in the corner: Harlan and Vey, Cargo
Agents, Dock Street. She knew what it said. Or she knew
it said one of two things, and either one would be a
door, and she did not know which side of the door she
wanted to be standing on. If it said no, she could keep
the stone on it forever. If it said yes, someone would
have to tell him, and the someone would be her.
"Ruth Ann's heavy," her father said.
"Is she?"
"Look at her waterline." He jerked his chin. "Dan
Pruett will want hands Saturday for the gutting. I told
him you'd come."
He had told Dan Pruett. Of course he had. He had
told Dan Pruett on Tuesday, probably, the same afternoon
the postman came down the cliff path, waving the cream
envelope above his head like a flag for her to see from
the beach, and her father had watched him come all the
way down and said nothing at all. Saturday. He had built
her a Saturday and set it on the calendar like a stone
on a letter.
She could have been angry. She tried it for a
moment, the way you try a plank before you put your
weight on it, and found it would not hold. Because he
was not wrong about her knots. Because the net in her
lap was one she had mended every spring since she was
nine, and she knew it the way she knew her own teeth
with her tongue. Because when he took the twine from her
fingers his own fingers had been warm, and she had
wanted, absurdly, for him to keep holding it.
The tide turned at four. The wind came round and
lifted one corner of the envelope, and it fluttered
under the stone like something breathing. Her father's
needle stopped. Nell watched his hands lie still on the
mesh for the space of three waves. Then they began
again, over, under, through, and he said, not looking
up, "You'll want to read that before the light goes."
"Tomorrow," she said.
He nodded as though she had told him the weather.
She pulled the next knot tight, too tight, and did not
let him see her loosen it.

In this passage from Salt Hours, Orla Bressan shows that Nell is torn between the future the letter promises and the love and duty that keep her beside her father. She feels resentment toward him for deciding things for her, but she also feels tenderness, and the author uses symbols, imagery, and the structure of the scene to show both feelings pulling at once.

The most important symbol is the stone on the letter. The narrator says it has a white band "like a wedding ring somebody had forgotten to take off," which makes it seem like a promise that is still holding on. Nell says the stone is only there because of the wind, but the narrator points out that "she told herself that was the only reason." This shows that she is hiding from herself. She is the one who has kept the letter from being read, so she is partly responsible for her own delay. Later the narrator compares the Saturday work to this stone when it says her father "built her a Saturday and set it on the calendar like a stone on a letter." The repeated stone image links Nell and her father, because both are weighing down the future in different ways.

The net is another image of being joined. Nell and her father are "joined by forty feet of brown mesh," which can feel like closeness but also like being tied together. The repeated phrase "over, under, through" also makes the work feel endless, like a routine she can't leave. It is comforting because it is familiar, but it is also trapping. Her mother's death is described with the image of mending a hole "by working inward from the sound edges," which suggests that Nell has always filled in what is missing for her father, so leaving would make a new hole.

Nell's feelings about her father are shown through the "Because" sequence. She tries to be angry about Saturday, but the anger "would not hold" like a bad plank. She lists reasons why she cannot be angry, such as the knots and the warmth of his fingers. This shows she is not able to simply see him as someone who controls her. Even when he takes the twine in "a quick small violence of the thumbs" she still wants him to keep holding it.

The ending shows the conflict best. Her father's needle stops when the wind lifts the envelope, and then he tells her she will want to read it. This is a change, because he seems to give her permission instead of telling her what to do. Nell answers "Tomorrow," and then she pulls a knot "too tight" and hides loosening it. The tight knot shows her tension, and the loosening shows she is trying to keep the peace and not let him see. Overall, Bressan shows that for Nell both leaving and staying are hard, and her love for her father makes the choice harder.

parts.prompt:
In many works of fiction, characters hold a secret together. The secret might be a crime two siblings both saw, a love affair a household agrees to ignore, or a family's hidden origins kept from the neighbors. Knowing the same thing that no one else knows can tie people together more closely than blood or vows. That same knowledge can also cut them off from everyone outside the circle, and sometimes from each other, because each person has to watch what the others might say. A secret held in common can be a refuge and a cell at once, and that tension often shows what a work believes about loyalty, honesty and belonging.

Either from your own reading or from the list below, choose a work of fiction in which characters are bound together by a shared secret that also isolates them. Then, in a well-written essay, analyze how the shared secret and its complex effects on those who keep it contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Do not merely summarize the plot.

Your essay should:
- State a defensible thesis about how the idea in the prompt contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole.
- Support the argument with specific, accurate evidence from the work you chose, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Do not merely summarize the plot.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

At the start of Macbeth, the Macbeths may be the closest couple in all of Shakespeare. He writes to his wife about the witches before he tells anyone else, and she reads his ambition better than he does. The murder of Duncan should seal that closeness, since now two people share something no one else in Scotland knows. Instead Shakespeare shows the secret slowly turning their marriage from a partnership into two separate cells. Because keeping a murder hidden depends on controlling what you say, even to the person who helped you, the bond that the secret creates is also what wears it away. The play suggests that loyalty built on concealment cannot last, because it needs the same silence that destroys it.

The binding effect is clearest on the night of the murder. Macbeth comes back carrying the bloody daggers, too shaken to return them, and Lady Macbeth takes them back herself and smears the sleeping grooms with blood. In this scene their roles fit together. Her nerve covers for his panic, and his act makes her plan real. Shakespeare even shows them finishing each other's thoughts in short, broken exchanges, so the rhythm of the dialogue makes them sound like one mind split between two voices. Blood is the symbol that joins them, because they both have it on their hands. Then the knocking at the gate interrupts them, a reminder that the outside world is right there. The secret only exists because there is a "them" and an "everyone else," so from the first scene their closeness and their isolation from Scotland are the same thing.

The isolation starts to turn inward once Macbeth becomes king. He arranges Banquo's murder without telling his wife and keeps her in the dark on purpose, which reverses the letter from Act 1. He might think he is protecting her, but the effect is that the secret now has layers, and she is outside one of them. At the banquet, when Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost, Lady Macbeth covers for him again, explaining his fits to the lords and then sending the guests away. On the surface this looks like the daggers scene repeated, but it is hollow. She is defending a crime she wasn't told about, and the guests leave suspicious. Her loyalty is now just damage control, and the dramatic irony (we know what Macbeth sees and she does not) shows how far apart they have grown while still standing next to each other.

By Act 5 the secret has fully separated them. Lady Macbeth sleepwalks, trying to wash blood off her hands that is no longer there, while a doctor and a gentlewoman listen. Someone could read this as the secret finally coming out, almost a confession that might bring relief. That reading doesn't hold up, though, because she says it alone, asleep, to people she can't see, and it frees nothing. It is the opposite of the night of the murder: then they shared one secret between two people, and now each carries a private version of it. When Macbeth hears she has died, he responds with numb exhaustion instead of grief, saying life means nothing. The man who once wrote to her first now hardly reacts to her death.

Shakespeare's tragedy shows that a secret can make a couple feel closer than anyone else, but only by cutting them off from everyone around them, and in the end from each other. In a play where killing a king upsets the whole natural order, it makes sense that the Macbeths' private loyalty grows into a kind of disorder too. The partnership was real, but because it depended on silence, it was ruining itself from the beginning.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis names a work of fiction in which a secret is shared by two or more characters and makes a claim about how that secret, through its binding or isolating effects or both, contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Simply saying that a secret exists, or restating the prompt, does not earn the point. A thesis about a secret kept by only one person qualifies only if it shows that others are bound into it. The claim may be in one or more sentences anywhere in the response.

Strong responses use specific references to the work: scenes where the secret is formed, tested or nearly exposed, and moments where keepers are drawn closer or set apart. Commentary should explain how these moments show both the bond and the isolation, and how the two connect to the work's larger meaning about loyalty, truth or belonging. For 4 points, the line of reasoning must be consistent and the evidence must be analyzed rather than summarized. For 3 points, the commentary is mostly relevant but uneven. Responses that mostly summarize the plot score no higher than 2.

Sophistication can be shown by exploring the paradox that the bond depends on the isolation, by placing the secret within the work's social or historical tensions, by weighing competing readings of whether disclosure is redemptive, or by sustaining a vivid, controlled style. A single passing gesture toward complexity does not earn the point.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In Macbeth, the murder of King Duncan is a secret that Macbeth and Lady Macbeth hold together, and it works as both a bond and a prison. Shakespeare uses their shared guilt to suggest that loyalty built on a crime cannot last, because the secret that joins them also cuts them off from the rest of Scotland and finally from each other. The play argues that a bond founded on hidden wrongdoing destroys the very closeness it seems to create.

At first the secret clearly brings the couple together. Lady Macbeth is the one who pushes her husband to kill Duncan, and when he hesitates she questions his manhood and makes the plan herself. After the murder, when Macbeth comes back with the daggers still in his hands, she takes them and returns them to the chamber to smear the guards with blood. In this scene they act almost as one person, and the quick, short exchanges between them show how much they depend on each other. The secret makes them partners, and their marriage seems stronger than it was before.

However, Shakespeare also shows the isolation starting right away. Macbeth says he heard voices saying that he would sleep no more, which shows that the guilt is already separating him from ordinary life. At the banquet, when he sees Banquo's ghost, nobody else can see it, so he looks mad in front of the lords. Lady Macbeth has to cover for him and send the guests away, and she is angry at him for nearly giving the secret away. Here the same secret that joined them makes each one a danger to the other, since one slip from either could expose them both. The ghost is also a good example of how Shakespeare uses the supernatural to show a private conscience that no one else can share.

By the end the couple are completely separated even though they still share the same knowledge. Macbeth goes on to have Banquo and Macduff's family killed without telling his wife, so he is acting alone. Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and tries to wash imaginary blood from her hands, and she speaks the secret aloud while the doctor and her gentlewoman listen. When she dies, Macbeth hardly seems to react, and his speech about life being meaningless shows how empty he has become. The secret that once tied them together has left each of them alone.

Overall, the shared secret shows what the play believes about loyalty and truth. The Macbeths are loyal to each other at the start, but it is a loyalty that depends on lying to everyone else, and so it cannot survive. The play suggests that real belonging needs honesty, and that a secret like theirs can only make a person more and more alone.

prompt.lead: In many works of fiction, characters hold a secret together. The secret might be a crime two siblings both saw, a love affair a household agrees to ignore, or a family's hidden origins kept from the neighbors. Knowing the same thing that no one else knows can tie people together more closely than blood or vows. That same knowledge can also cut them off from everyone outside the circle, and sometimes from each other, because each person has to watch what the others might say. A secret held in common can be a refuge and a cell at once, and that tension often shows what a work believes about loyalty, honesty and belonging.
prompt.task: Either from your own reading or from the list below, choose a work of fiction in which characters are bound together by a shared secret that also isolates them. Then, in a well-written essay, analyze how the shared secret and its complex effects on those who keep it contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Do not merely summarize the plot.
requirements: State a defensible thesis about how the idea in the prompt contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole.
Support the argument with specific, accurate evidence from the work you chose, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Do not merely summarize the plot.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis names a work of fiction in which a secret is shared by two or more characters and makes a claim about how that secret, through its binding or isolating effects or both, contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Simply saying that a secret exists, or restating the prompt, does not earn the point. A thesis about a secret kept by only one person qualifies only if it shows that others are bound into it. The claim may be in one or more sentences anywhere in the response.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses use specific references to the work: scenes where the secret is formed, tested or nearly exposed, and moments where keepers are drawn closer or set apart. Commentary should explain how these moments show both the bond and the isolation, and how the two connect to the work's larger meaning about loyalty, truth or belonging. For 4 points, the line of reasoning must be consistent and the evidence must be analyzed rather than summarized. For 3 points, the commentary is mostly relevant but uneven. Responses that mostly summarize the plot score no higher than 2.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication can be shown by exploring the paradox that the bond depends on the isolation, by placing the secret within the work's social or historical tensions, by weighing competing readings of whether disclosure is redemptive, or by sustaining a vivid, controlled style. A single passing gesture toward complexity does not earn the point.

scoring_notes: Any work of fiction of literary merit is acceptable: a novel, a play or an extended short story from any period or culture.
The secret must be shared or must bind more than one character. Readers should not reward responses that fail to establish this.
Accuracy about the chosen work matters only insofar as errors undermine the argument.
Do not penalize a response for arguing that one effect, binding or isolating, outweighs the other, as long as it engages both.

For the literary argument question the evidence comes from the work the student chooses: it must be specific and accurate, and the commentary must explain how the named concept contributes to an interpretation of the whole work rather than summarize the plot.

lines_of_reasoning: The secret creates a private language or ritual among the keepers that excludes outsiders. Fits novels about siblings or childhood friends who witnessed a death.
The secret binds a family but cuts it off from the community. Fits family sagas that hide an ancestor's crime or mixed parentage, and colonial-era or diaspora novels about concealed identity.
Keeping the secret slowly turns the bond into mutual surveillance, which isolates the keepers from each other. Fits crime novels where accomplices grow paranoid, and tragedies of conspiracy.
A secret that protects a vulnerable person becomes a moral burden on the protectors. Fits novels about hiding refugees, fugitives or enslaved people seeking freedom.
Revealing the secret breaks the bond and also frees the keepers, so the work sets truth against belonging. Fits domestic dramas and confession narratives.
The secret marks a class, gender or generational divide: those who know hold power over those who do not. Fits novels of manners and boarding-school novels.
Outsiders sense the secret without knowing it, which deepens the keepers' isolation. Fits small-town fiction and ghost stories.
defensible_positions: The shared secret holds a fragile community together but finally shows that intimacy built on concealment cannot last.
The work treats the secret as a necessary shelter against a hostile society, and the isolation it causes is a cost worth paying.
The secret isolates the keepers less from the world than from their own past selves, which suggests that identity depends on what one can say aloud.
common_pitfalls: Retelling the plot of how the secret was formed and revealed without analyzing its effects.
Treating the secret as only binding or only isolating, which ignores the tension the prompt asks for.
Forcing a work with a merely private secret (one person alone) to fit the shared-secret requirement.
Discussing the secret without connecting it to the meaning of the work as a whole.
Writing about several works superficially instead of one in depth.

samples.essay:
At the start of Macbeth, the Macbeths may be the closest couple in all of Shakespeare. He writes to his wife about the witches before he tells anyone else, and she reads his ambition better than he does. The murder of Duncan should seal that closeness, since now two people share something no one else in Scotland knows. Instead Shakespeare shows the secret slowly turning their marriage from a partnership into two separate cells. Because keeping a murder hidden depends on controlling what you say, even to the person who helped you, the bond that the secret creates is also what wears it away. The play suggests that loyalty built on concealment cannot last, because it needs the same silence that destroys it.

The binding effect is clearest on the night of the murder. Macbeth comes back carrying the bloody daggers, too shaken to return them, and Lady Macbeth takes them back herself and smears the sleeping grooms with blood. In this scene their roles fit together. Her nerve covers for his panic, and his act makes her plan real. Shakespeare even shows them finishing each other's thoughts in short, broken exchanges, so the rhythm of the dialogue makes them sound like one mind split between two voices. Blood is the symbol that joins them, because they both have it on their hands. Then the knocking at the gate interrupts them, a reminder that the outside world is right there. The secret only exists because there is a "them" and an "everyone else," so from the first scene their closeness and their isolation from Scotland are the same thing.

The isolation starts to turn inward once Macbeth becomes king. He arranges Banquo's murder without telling his wife and keeps her in the dark on purpose, which reverses the letter from Act 1. He might think he is protecting her, but the effect is that the secret now has layers, and she is outside one of them. At the banquet, when Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost, Lady Macbeth covers for him again, explaining his fits to the lords and then sending the guests away. On the surface this looks like the daggers scene repeated, but it is hollow. She is defending a crime she wasn't told about, and the guests leave suspicious. Her loyalty is now just damage control, and the dramatic irony (we know what Macbeth sees and she does not) shows how far apart they have grown while still standing next to each other.

By Act 5 the secret has fully separated them. Lady Macbeth sleepwalks, trying to wash blood off her hands that is no longer there, while a doctor and a gentlewoman listen. Someone could read this as the secret finally coming out, almost a confession that might bring relief. That reading doesn't hold up, though, because she says it alone, asleep, to people she can't see, and it frees nothing. It is the opposite of the night of the murder: then they shared one secret between two people, and now each carries a private version of it. When Macbeth hears she has died, he responds with numb exhaustion instead of grief, saying life means nothing. The man who once wrote to her first now hardly reacts to her death.

Shakespeare's tragedy shows that a secret can make a couple feel closer than anyone else, but only by cutting them off from everyone around them, and in the end from each other. In a play where killing a king upsets the whole natural order, it makes sense that the Macbeths' private loyalty grows into a kind of disorder too. The partnership was real, but because it depended on silence, it was ruining itself from the beginning.

In Macbeth, the murder of King Duncan is a secret that Macbeth and Lady Macbeth hold together, and it works as both a bond and a prison. Shakespeare uses their shared guilt to suggest that loyalty built on a crime cannot last, because the secret that joins them also cuts them off from the rest of Scotland and finally from each other. The play argues that a bond founded on hidden wrongdoing destroys the very closeness it seems to create.

At first the secret clearly brings the couple together. Lady Macbeth is the one who pushes her husband to kill Duncan, and when he hesitates she questions his manhood and makes the plan herself. After the murder, when Macbeth comes back with the daggers still in his hands, she takes them and returns them to the chamber to smear the guards with blood. In this scene they act almost as one person, and the quick, short exchanges between them show how much they depend on each other. The secret makes them partners, and their marriage seems stronger than it was before.

However, Shakespeare also shows the isolation starting right away. Macbeth says he heard voices saying that he would sleep no more, which shows that the guilt is already separating him from ordinary life. At the banquet, when he sees Banquo's ghost, nobody else can see it, so he looks mad in front of the lords. Lady Macbeth has to cover for him and send the guests away, and she is angry at him for nearly giving the secret away. Here the same secret that joined them makes each one a danger to the other, since one slip from either could expose them both. The ghost is also a good example of how Shakespeare uses the supernatural to show a private conscience that no one else can share.

By the end the couple are completely separated even though they still share the same knowledge. Macbeth goes on to have Banquo and Macduff's family killed without telling his wife, so he is acting alone. Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and tries to wash imaginary blood from her hands, and she speaks the secret aloud while the doctor and her gentlewoman listen. When she dies, Macbeth hardly seems to react, and his speech about life being meaningless shows how empty he has become. The secret that once tied them together has left each of them alone.

Overall, the shared secret shows what the play believes about loyalty and truth. The Macbeths are loyal to each other at the start, but it is a loyalty that depends on lying to everyone else, and so it cannot survive. The play suggests that real belonging needs honesty, and that a secret like theirs can only make a person more and more alone.
